title: Mixtures
competency: Describe and classify mixtures as homogeneous and heterogeneous.

keywords.def: A physical combination of two or more pure substances; each keeps its own properties.
A mixture with the same composition throughout and no visible boundary. Also called a solution.
A mixture with no uniform composition; its parts can be seen.
Another name for a homogeneous mixture, like salt water.

en.text: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more pure substances. Each substance keeps its own properties, because they are mixed, not chemically joined. Salt and sand mixed together are still salt and sand. Soil, cooking oil, ink, milk and air are mixtures.

screens.title: Salt and sand
screens.ask: Hiwot mixes rock salt crystals with sand. Is the salt still salt?
screens.after:
Yes. Mixing does not change the salt or the sand.
The salt still tastes salty and dissolves in water. The sand does not.
Each keeps its own properties. That is a mixture.

screens.title: 2.3.3 Mixtures
paras: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more pure substances.
Each substance keeps its own properties.
They are physically mixed, not chemically combined.

screens.title: Common mixtures
screens.ask: Tap each mixture to see what is in it.
items: Particles of different sizes and plant material.
Dyes dissolved in alcohol and water.
Proteins, carbohydrates, fats, water and minerals.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A physical combination of two or more pure substances; each keeps its own properties.

screens.text: Is air a pure substance or a mixture?
opts: Pure substance: it is one gas
screens.why:
Air contains oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and more.
These gases are only physically mixed, not joined.
So air is a mixture, not a pure substance.
It is not oxygen only: most of the air is nitrogen.

screens.text: True or false? In a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties.
screens.why:
In a mixture the substances are not chemically joined.
In Experiment 2.2 Part I, iron in the iron–sulfur mixture still sticks to a magnet.
So each substance keeps its properties: true.

screens.text: Mixture or compound? Which is true for a mixture but NOT for a compound?
opts: Its parts keep their own properties and can be separated physically
It can only be split chemically
screens.ans: Its parts keep their own properties and can be separated physically
screens.why:
In a mixture nothing is joined, so each part keeps its properties.
That is why a mixture can be separated by physical means (like a magnet).
New properties, a fixed composition and splitting only by chemical means describe a compound.
So the answer is: its parts keep their properties and can be separated physically.

en.text: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout and no visible boundary. It is also called a solution, like salt water or air. A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform and its parts can be seen, like soil, blood, milk, or oil and water.

screens.title: Can you see the parts?
screens.ask: Which one has parts you can see?
screens.after:
Sand in water: you can see the sand grains at the bottom.
Sugar dissolves completely, so sugar water looks the same everywhere.
Air is a mixture of gases you cannot see apart.

screens.title: Homogeneous mixtures
paras: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout. It has no visible boundary.
It is also called a solution.
Salt water is the same salt-water mix in every part.
Solutions can be solid, liquid or gas.

screens.title: Table 2.4 Types of homogeneous mixture (solution)
screens.ask: Tap each type to see examples.
items: State: gas. Example: air (oxygen and nitrogen).
State: liquid. Example: soft drinks such as Pepsi, Mirinda, Coca-Cola.
State: liquid. Example: alcohol in water.
State: liquid. Examples: salt solution, sugar solution.
State: solid. Examples: brass (zinc and copper), bronze (copper and tin).

screens.title: Heterogeneous mixtures
paras: A heterogeneous mixture has no uniform composition. It has visible boundaries.
We can see its parts by eye, or with a microscope or magnifying glass.
Examples: sulfur and iron filings, blood, milk, sand and water, muddy water, oil and water, dusty air, soil.

screens.title: Table 2.5 Homogeneous and heterogeneous
table: Sugar solution, soft drinks, salt solution
Milk, soil, sand and water, oil and water

screens.title: Homogeneous or heterogeneous? Tap each part.
sets: Uniform composition, one phase, parts not easily seen. "Homo" means the same. Examples: sugar solution, soft drinks, salt solution.
Non-uniform composition, two or more phases, parts easily seen. "Hetero" means different. Examples: milk, soil, sand and water, oil and water.
overlaps: Both are mixtures. Each substance keeps its own properties, and the parts can be separated by physical means.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A mixture with the same composition throughout and no visible boundary. Also called a solution.
A mixture with no uniform composition; its parts can be seen.
Another name for a homogeneous mixture, like salt water.

screens.text: Which substance makes a homogeneous mixture (a solution) with water?
screens.why:
A homogeneous mixture forms when a substance dissolves completely.
Sugar dissolves in water and makes a sugar solution.
Oil and benzene form a layer on water. Sulfur does not dissolve.
So the answer is sugar.

items: Gas in gas: the same everywhere.
You can see pieces of different sizes.
Salt is dissolved: solid in liquid.
The book lists blood as heterogeneous. Under a microscope its parts can be seen.
Zinc and copper mixed evenly: solid in solid.
Oil floats on water as a separate layer.
screens.why:
Ask: does it look the same everywhere?
Yes → homogeneous: air, salt solution, brass.
No, parts or layers can be seen → heterogeneous: soil, blood, oil and water.
screens.clue: Are there layers or visible bits?
screens.text: Sort each mixture: homogeneous or heterogeneous?
True or false? A heterogeneous mixture contains only one phase.
screens.why:
A heterogeneous mixture has visible boundaries between its parts.
Each visible part is a phase, so it has two or more phases.
Example: oil and water form two layers.
Only a homogeneous mixture has one phase. So false.

screens.text: Name the type of solution: Pepsi is a homogeneous mixture of which type?
screens.why:
The bubbles in Pepsi are carbon dioxide gas.
The gas is dissolved in a liquid drink.
So it is a gas-in-liquid solution (Table 2.4).

screens.text: Solutions and mixtures: which statement is correct?
opts: Every solution is a homogeneous mixture
screens.ans: Every solution is a homogeneous mixture
screens.why:
The book: a homogeneous mixture is also called a solution. So every solution is homogeneous.
Milk is heterogeneous, so it is not a solution.
Brass is homogeneous (solid in solid).
Air is a mixture, not a pure substance.

items.title: I Q1. Classify (a–g)
items: A metal element: one kind of atom.
Many substances mixed; parts seen under a microscope.
Pure ethanol is one compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Salt water with many dissolved substances.
A metal element: one kind of atom.
Sodium chloride: sodium and chlorine joined.
items.why:
Element: one kind of atom.
Compound: elements chemically joined, a pure substance.
Mixture: substances physically mixed.
First ask: is it pure or a mixture? If pure, ask: one kind of atom or more?
Here: uranium and iron are elements; water, alcohol and table salt are compounds; blood and the oceans are mixtures.
items.text: Classify each substance as an element, a compound or a mixture.

items.title: I Q1. Classify (h–n)
items: Zinc and copper mixed together (a solid solution).
A gas element: one kind of atom.
A metal element: one kind of atom.
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined.
items.why:
Element: one kind of atom.
Compound: elements chemically joined, a pure substance.
Mixture: substances physically mixed.
First ask: is it pure or a mixture? If pure, ask: one kind of atom or more?
Here: hydrogen and gold are elements; sugar and benzene are compounds; brass, milk and honey are mixtures.
items.text: Classify each substance as an element, a compound or a mixture.
Which of the following is a metallic liquid element at room temperature?
items.why:
Metals are solid at room temperature, except mercury.
Bromine is also liquid, but it is a non-metal.
Sodium and iron are solid metals.
So the answer is mercury.

items.text: Identify the type of element: Substance Y is a hard, lustrous solid which readily conducts heat and electricity. Y is likely to be:
items.why:
Lustrous means shiny.
Hard, shiny and a good conductor of heat and electricity: these are metal properties (Table 2.3).
Non-metals are dull and poor conductors.
So Y is a metal.

items.text: Which substance makes a homogeneous mixture (a solution) with water?
items.why:
Sugar dissolves completely in water: one phase, a solution.
Oil and benzene stay as a separate layer.
Sulfur does not dissolve.
So the answer is sugar.

items.text: Which of the following substances is not a mixture?
items.why:
Air is a mixture of gases. Sea water has salts dissolved in water.
Brass is a mixture of zinc and copper.
Pure water is one compound only (hydrogen and oxygen joined).
So pure water is not a mixture.

items.text: Which of these are homogeneous mixtures?
items.why:
A homogeneous mixture looks the same everywhere (one phase).
Air, salt solution, sugar solution and Pepsi are solutions. Brass is a solid-in-solid solution.
Milk and soil have visible parts: heterogeneous.
Water and gold are pure substances, not mixtures at all.
items.clue: Mixtures that look the same everywhere.

items.text: Which of these are heterogeneous mixtures?
items.why:
A heterogeneous mixture has parts you can see.
The book names milk and soil as heterogeneous.
Bronze, air and ink are homogeneous (solutions).
Ethanol and iron are pure substances, not mixtures.
items.clue: Mixtures whose parts can be seen.

test.text: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
test.why:
Sea water, bronze and air are uniform: homogeneous.
Blood has parts that can be seen under a microscope.
The book lists blood as heterogeneous.

test.text: True or false? A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution.
test.why:
A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout.
The book says it is also called a solution, like salt water.
So the statement is true.

test.text: Find the odd one out: all of these are heterogeneous mixtures EXCEPT …
test.why:
Soil, water and oil, and blood all have visible parts or layers: heterogeneous.
In salt solution the salt is fully dissolved. It looks the same everywhere.
So salt solution is the homogeneous one.

test.text: Classify brass: brass (zinc and copper) is a …
test.why:
Brass is zinc and copper mixed evenly.
It looks the same throughout, so it is homogeneous.
Both parts are solids: a solid-in-solid solution (Table 2.4).
It is not a compound, because the metals are not chemically joined.

test.text: Mixture or compound? Which shows a mixture, not a compound?
opts: Iron filings and sulfur that a magnet can separate
Water made of hydrogen and oxygen
test.ans: Iron filings and sulfur that a magnet can separate
test.why:
In a mixture each part keeps its properties.
Iron filings and sulfur: the magnet still pulls out the iron. So it is a mixture.
Water, table salt and iron sulfide are compounds: their elements are chemically joined.
